ascetic

uh-SET-ik · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Ascetic is practicing severe self-discipline and abstaining from worldly pleasures, especially for spiritual reasons.

The monk's ascetic lifestyle -- one meal a day, no possessions beyond a robe and a bowl -- had lasted for over thirty years.

Example

Long before he became a wealthy tech founder, he lived an almost ascetic student life, sleeping on a mattress on the floor and eating the same simple meal every night.

Ascetic describes a deliberate, disciplined rejection of comfort and luxury -- not poverty forced by circumstance, but a chosen simplicity.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

austere: Austere describes conditions and surfaces -- a bare cell, a plain gray suit, a strict manner -- severity in how things look and feel. Ascetic describes a person's chosen practice of self-denial, usually for spiritual or moral reasons. A room is austere; the monk who chose it is ascetic.

abstemious: Abstemious is self-restraint at the table -- eating and drinking sparingly on principle. It is narrower than ascetic: an abstemious person limits only food and drink, while an ascetic renounces comfort across a whole way of life.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

hedonistic: devoted to the pursuit of pleasure

indulgent: allowing oneself pleasures freely (a word you met earlier in this course)

Where it sits · how severely comforts are given up

frugal → ascetic → self-mortifying

frugal vs. ascetic: Frugal (a word you met earlier in this course) means careful with money or resources, without necessarily being tied to spiritual discipline the way ascetic is.

self-mortifying vs. ascetic: Self-mortifying is more extreme than ascetic: an ascetic gives up worldly comforts, but the self-mortifying go further, deliberately inflicting suffering on themselves as spiritual discipline.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — ascet-: exercise, training, especially spiritual or moral discipline (from Greek askesis, 'training,' and asketes, 'one who trains')

Suffix — -ic: characteristic of (Greek)

Put it together: Ascetic comes from Greek askesis, 'exercise' or 'training': ascet- (from asketes, 'one who trains') + -ic ('characteristic of'). Originally used for athletes' physical training, it was later applied to the rigorous spiritual 'training' of self-denial -- an ascetic lifestyle is one disciplined through deliberate self-denial.

Use the root in a new word: asceticism: The religious order was famous for its extreme asceticism, requiring members to fast for weeks at a time.
